newsitem.title: TURKEY: Power struggle at heart of Turkey political crisis.
newsitem.headline: Power struggle at heart of Turkey political crisis.

text.p: Mesut Yilmaz is an introvert, slow in action and speech. Bitter rival Tansu Ciller is a political gambler renowned for thinking on her feet and outbursts of fiery temper.
A power struggle between the two strong-willed conservatives is fuelling Turkey's 18-month-old political crisis and giving the embattled Islamists room to breathe, analysts say.

Their frequent disagreements helped outgoing Islamist Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan into power last year. A fresh round of the feud is an obstacle in the way of a secularist pact against an Islamist return to office.
"(The Islam-based) Welfare Party wouldn't be so important if the conservatives united," a Western diplomat said.
"The way to stop Erbakan is to send the pair of them to a desert island and let someone else take over," he said.
The two were at odds again on Tuesday at a brief meeting arranged only after Yilmaz, the new prime minister-designate, sent Ciller a bouquet of lilies in a peace gesture.
Ciller, miffed at Yilmaz's appointment, was unswayed. She refused to even talk about an effort by her opponent to woo her away from a pro-Islamic alliance.
"I did not discuss the government issue, so as not to legitimise Yilmaz's position," she said.

Erbakan, facing secularist pressure, resigned last week under a plan that called for his coalition partner, Ciller, to lead the nation to early elections. But instead President Suleyman Demirel chose Yilmaz to form a new government.
Pro-Western technocrat Ciller says she would rather stay loyal to the Islamists.
She had dropped strong criticism of the Islamists last year and joined them in office after Yilmaz backed corruption charges against her when they were in a conservative coalition together.
Analysts say Ciller is waiting for Yilmaz to fail so that Demirel will give her a chance.
The electoral power of the right is almost double that of Erbakan's Islamists, who narrowly won the last general elections in late 1995 with 21 percent of the vote.
Analysts, however, say the conservatives will stay split until one of the pair emerges as undisputed head of a united grouping.
"This is a struggle to the death because they both know their survival depends on it. One of them will become the leader of the centre-right," said Sedat Erin, a columnist for the Hurriyet daily.
"Erbakan would never have become prime minister if it hadn't been for the fight between them."
The opposing personalities play a role in the rivalry.
"I think Yilmaz just can't stand Ciller," said political commentator Bilal Cetin. "It might be something to do with her being a woman and being more successful in politics."
Little seems to stir emotions in Yilmaz, staid leader of the Motherland Party, except the prospect of being left behind by the rapid rise of his nemesis.
"It is my mission to wipe Tansu Ciller out of politics," he said earlier this month. Yilmaz has spent most of the 1990s in opposition, apart from two brief spells as prime minister.
Ciller, currently the second-in-charge of a caretaker government, has been in office since becoming Turkey's first woman leader in 1993.
Despite her rejection on Tuesday, Ciller left the door open for future cooperation between the two -- under her leadership.
Yilmaz has the backing of left-wing MPs but he needs the support of a dozen more deputies to guarantee winning a parliamentary vote of confidence in any anti-Islamist government he can form.
The right could probably win the vote even without leftist support if they united.
Said the Western diplomat: "Turkey is a conservative country that votes conservative but is denied a true expression of its will."
